categories.label: Competitions
categories.note: Contests and olympiads, from school rounds to national teams.

categories.label: Summer programs
categories.note: Residential and online programs that run over the summer.

categories.label: Internships
categories.note: Paid and unpaid work with a lab, company or organization.

categories.label: Fellowships
categories.note: Funding and a cohort for students doing their own work.

categories.label: Scholarships
categories.note: Money for college, from national awards to engineering societies.

categories.label: Events
categories.note: Hackathons, conferences, festivals and citizen science.

categories.label: Clubs & free learning
categories.note: Math circles, clubs, and free courses and practice online.

programs.title: USA Computing Olympiad (USACO)
programs.summary: Online programming contests in four divisions: Bronze, Silver, Gold and Platinum. Students move up a division by scoring well. The US Open and the training camp are by invitation, based on the online contests.
body: Gold and Platinum results only count for promotion to camp if the student takes the contest at the certified start time. The 2026-27 dates are not posted yet, so the timeline uses last season's dates moved forward a year.
programs.when: Three online contests in January and February, then the US Open

programs.title: AMC 10 and AMC 12
programs.summary: The first round of the US math olympiad track. AMC 10 is for grade 10 and below, AMC 12 for grade 12 and below. Students take it through a school or competition manager, so the school has to register first.
body: High scorers qualify for the AIME. From 2027 the AIME is taken at Pearson testing centers, and students schedule and pay for it themselves.
programs.when: AMC in November, AIME in February
timeline: Late registration closes, returning schools only
programs.format: In person, at a school or test site

programs.title: Regeneron Science Talent Search
programs.summary: A research competition for seniors in US high schools. Students submit their own original research with a long written application. Team projects are not allowed.
body: The top 300 scholars get $2,000, and so do their schools. The 40 finalists get at least $25,000 and spend a week in Washington, DC. First place is $250,000.
programs.when: Applications due in early November of senior year

programs.title: AMC 8
programs.summary: A 25-question, 40-minute multiple choice test for students in grade 8 and below. It is often a student's first national math contest.
body: Award: Certificates and honor roll.
Who can apply: Grade 8 and below.
programs.when: Registration in the fall; test usually in late January
programs.format: In person, At your school or a registered host site

programs.title: American Invitational Mathematics Examination (AIME)
programs.summary: A 15-question, 3-hour test with integer answers from 0 to 999, for top AMC 10 and AMC 12 scorers. AIME and AMC scores together decide who is invited to the USAMO and USAJMO.
body: Award: Qualification for USAMO or USAJMO.
Who can apply: Invitation based on AMC 10/12 score.
programs.when: By qualification; test usually in early February
programs.format: In person, At your school or a host site

programs.title: USA Mathematical Olympiad (USAMO)
programs.summary: Six proof problems over two days for the top AMC 12 and AIME scorers. The top scorers are invited to the Mathematical Olympiad Program.
body: Award: Awards to top scorers; path to MOP and the IMO team.
Who can apply: US and Canadian students, invited by AMC 12 plus AIME index.

programs.title: USA Junior Mathematical Olympiad (USAJMO)
programs.summary: The same format as the USAMO, six proof problems over two days, for top students who qualified through the AMC 10 and AIME. Top scorers can be invited to MOP.
body: Who can apply: Grade 10 and below, invited by AMC 10 plus AIME index.

programs.title: Mathematical Olympiad Program (MOP)
programs.summary: A summer training camp of about four weeks for the top USAMO and USAJMO scorers. The US team for the International Mathematical Olympiad is picked through MOP and team selection tests.
body: Who can apply: Invitation based on olympiad results.

programs.title: International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO)
programs.summary: The main international math olympiad for high school students. Each country sends a team of up to six, who solve six proof problems over two days.
body: Award: Gold, silver and bronze medals.
Who can apply: Chosen onto the national team; under 20 and not yet in university.
programs.when: Team chosen in spring through the MAA olympiad pipeline; contest in July

programs.title: European Girls' Mathematical Olympiad (EGMO)
programs.summary: An international olympiad for teams of four girls, run like the IMO with six proof problems over two days. The US sends a team chosen through the MAA olympiad pipeline.
body: Award: Medals.
Who can apply: Chosen onto the US team.
programs.when: Team chosen in winter; contest usually in April

programs.title: MATHCOUNTS Competition Series
programs.summary: A middle school contest with school, chapter, state and national rounds. Students take written rounds and a head-to-head Countdown Round.
body: Award: Trophies and scholarships at nationals.
Who can apply: Grades 6 to 8.
programs.when: School registration in the fall; chapter contests in February, state in March, nationals in May

programs.title: Math Kangaroo USA
programs.summary: A 75-minute multiple choice contest for grades 1 to 12, part of an international contest held in many countries on the same day.
body: Award: Medals and prizes by grade.
programs.when: Register in the fall and winter; contest in March

programs.title: Harvard-MIT Mathematics Tournament (HMMT February)
programs.summary: A large team and individual tournament held at Harvard or MIT, with harder problems than most high school contests. Rounds include individual subject tests, a team round and a Guts round.
body: Who can apply: High school teams, capped in size.
programs.when: Registration opens in the fall; tournament in February
programs.format: In person, Harvard or MIT, Cambridge, MA

programs.title: HMMT November
programs.summary: HMMT's fall tournament, meant to be easier than the February event and a good first tournament for newer competitors. It has a general test, a theme round, a team round and a Guts round.
body: Who can apply: High school teams.
programs.when: Registration in early fall; tournament in November
programs.format: In person, Harvard or MIT, Cambridge, MA

programs.title: Princeton University Mathematics Competition (PUMaC)
programs.summary: A team tournament run by Princeton undergraduates, with individual subject tests in divisions A and B plus team, power and live rounds.
programs.when: Registration in early fall; tournament in November

programs.title: American Regions Mathematics League (ARML)
programs.summary: A team contest where 15-person teams from states, regions and cities compete on team, power, individual and relay rounds. It runs at several sites on the same weekend.
body: Who can apply: Chosen onto a regional team.
programs.when: Teams form through local math leagues in spring; contest in late May or early June
programs.format: In person, Several US university sites

programs.title: ARML Local
programs.summary: A shorter version of ARML that schools and clubs run at their own site with teams of up to six. Problems and scoring come from ARML.
programs.format: In person, At your school or club

programs.title: Berkeley Math Tournament (BMT)
programs.summary: A student-run team tournament at UC Berkeley with Power, Individual and Guts rounds. There is also a separate online version.
body: Who can apply: Grade 12 and below.
programs.when: November 14, 2026 in person; online version December 5, 2026

programs.title: Berkeley mini Math Tournament (BmMT)
programs.summary: A tournament for middle school students run by the Berkeley Math Tournament team, with Puzzle, Individual, Team and Relay rounds.
body: Who can apply: Grade 8 and below.
programs.when: Usually April; an online version is also offered

programs.title: Carnegie Mellon Informatics and Mathematics Competition (CMIMC)
programs.summary: A team contest run by CMU students with math rounds and a programming round. It is held in person at CMU and has an online option.

programs.title: Stanford Math Tournament (SMT)
programs.summary: A tournament run by Stanford students with subject tests, a team round, a Power round and a Guts round. There is an in-person event and an online event.

programs.title: Caltech Math Meet (formerly CHMMC)
programs.summary: A team competition for high school students run by Caltech students. It used to be called the Caltech Harvey Mudd Math Competition.
programs.when: Registration closes in November; contest usually in January

programs.title: Duke Math Meet
programs.summary: A regional contest for teams of six high school students, run by Duke undergraduates. Rounds cover algebra, geometry, number theory and counting.
body: Who can apply: Limited number of teams per club.

programs.title: Math Majors of America Tournament for High Schools (MMATHS)
programs.summary: A fall team tournament held at Yale and other university sites, with an individual round and a mixer round where teams are shuffled.
programs.when: Registration in early fall; tournament in the fall
programs.format: In person, Yale and other host sites

programs.title: Math League Contests
programs.summary: Short contests that schools give during the school year, with separate tests for grades 4 to 12. Students take them at school and results are ranked by state and region.
programs.when: School registration in the fall; contests through the school year

programs.title: Math Olympiads for Elementary and Middle Schools (MOEMS)
programs.summary: Five monthly contests from November to March, each with five problems in 30 minutes. Schools and clubs run them for grades 4 to 8.
body: Award: Patches, pins and trophies.
Who can apply: Division E: grades 4 to 6; Division M: grades 6 to 8.
programs.when: Register by the fall; contests November to March
programs.format: In person, At your school or club

programs.title: Math Prize for Girls
programs.summary: A 20-question, 150-minute contest for girls held each fall at MIT. Students qualify through their AMC 10 or AMC 12 score.
body: Award: Cash prizes for top scorers.
Who can apply: Girls in grade 12 and below with qualifying AMC scores.
programs.when: Apply in late spring and summer; contest in the fall

programs.title: USA Mathematical Talent Search (USAMTS)
programs.summary: A free contest where students write full proofs to five problems each round and have about a month per round. Graders send back written comments.
body: Award: Prizes for top scorers.
Who can apply: US middle and high school students.
programs.when: Rounds run from September to March; sign up by the first round

programs.title: Purple Comet! Math Meet
programs.summary: A free online team contest held each spring, with middle school and high school divisions. Teams of up to six work together at their school.
programs.when: Registration in winter; contest in April

programs.title: Noetic Math Contest
programs.summary: A 20-question, 45-minute contest for grades 2 to 8 that schools and families run twice a year.
body: Award: Honor roll certificates and medals.
programs.format: In person, At your school or home group

programs.title: New York City Interscholastic Math League (NYCIML)
programs.summary: A math league for New York City high schools. Teams take contests at member schools during the year.
body: Who can apply: NYC area schools.

programs.title: William Lowell Putnam Mathematical Competition
programs.summary: The main math contest for undergraduates in the US and Canada, with twelve proof problems. From 2026 it runs as four 90-minute sessions.
body: Award: Cash prizes for top students and teams.
Who can apply: Undergraduates at US and Canadian colleges.
programs.when: December 5, 2026; faculty supervisors register by November 15

programs.title: CEMC Mathematics Contests
programs.org: Centre for Education in Mathematics and Computing, University of Waterloo
programs.summary: Waterloo runs a set of math contests that US schools can also enter, including the Gauss, Pascal, Cayley, Fermat, Euclid and Canadian Team Mathematics Contest.
programs.when: Varies by contest, fall to spring

programs.title: Johns Hopkins Math Tournament (JHMT)
programs.summary: A student-run tournament for middle and high school students with teams of up to four, including team, individual and relay rounds.

programs.title: Brown University Math Olympiad (BrUMO)
programs.summary: A team math tournament for high school students run by Brown undergraduates.

programs.title: MATHCOUNTS National Math Club
programs.summary: A free program that gives schools and clubs monthly problem sets and activities. It has no competition pressure and clubs that meet a set number of times can earn recognition.
programs.format: In person, At your school or club

programs.title: USACO Training Camp and IOI team
programs.summary: Top Platinum students are invited to a summer training camp. The US team for the International Olympiad in Informatics is picked there.
body: Who can apply: US high school students, by invitation.
programs.when: By invitation after the US Open, spring

programs.title: International Olympiad in Informatics (IOI)
programs.summary: The main international programming olympiad for high school students. Each country sends up to four students, who solve algorithm problems over two contest days.
body: Award: Gold, silver and bronze medals.
Who can apply: Chosen onto the national team.
programs.when: US team chosen through USACO; contest in summer

programs.title: European Girls' Olympiad in Informatics (EGOI)
programs.summary: An international programming olympiad for teams of up to four girls. The US team is chosen through USACO results.
body: Award: Medals.
Who can apply: Chosen onto the US team.
programs.when: Team chosen in spring; contest in summer

programs.title: American Computer Science League (ACSL)
programs.summary: Schools give short contests during the year that mix written computer science questions with a programming problem. Top scorers go to an all-star final.
body: Who can apply: Divisions for elementary through senior high.
programs.when: School registration in the fall; contests from December to spring

programs.title: Canadian Computing Competition (CCC)
programs.org: Centre for Education in Mathematics and Computing, University of Waterloo
programs.summary: A 3-hour programming contest with Junior and Senior levels. Schools outside Canada, including US schools, can register students.

programs.title: International Collegiate Programming Contest (ICPC)
programs.summary: A team programming contest for university students. Teams of three share one computer, compete in regional contests in the fall, and the best teams go to the World Finals.
body: Who can apply: University students, teams of three with a coach.

programs.title: Congressional App Challenge
programs.summary: Students build an app on any platform and submit it to their member of Congress. Each participating district picks a winner, whose app can be shown at the Capitol.
body: Award: District winners recognized and invited to a Capitol event.
Who can apply: Students in participating US congressional districts.
programs.when: Usually late October or early November

programs.title: Technovation Girls
programs.summary: Teams of girls spend a season learning to code, then build a mobile app or AI project to solve a problem in their community and write a business plan.
body: Who can apply: Girls ages 8 to 18.
programs.when: Season runs August to April; registration usually closes in March

programs.title: CALICO
programs.summary: An online programming contest for high school students run by Berkeley students, with teams solving algorithm problems of mixed difficulty.

programs.title: Lockheed Martin Code Quest
programs.summary: A programming contest where teams of up to three high school students solve problems in Java, C++ or Python. It is held at Lockheed Martin sites and online.
programs.format: Hybrid, Lockheed Martin sites in the US and abroad

programs.title: UIL Computer Science
programs.summary: A Texas school contest with a written test and a team programming round, going from district to regional to state.
body: Who can apply: Students at UIL member schools in Texas.
programs.when: District contests in spring; state in May

programs.title: Stanford ProCo
programs.summary: A programming contest for high school teams of up to three in the ICPC style, with Novice and Advanced divisions.

programs.title: PClassic
programs.summary: A programming contest for high school students run by Penn students, held in person and online.

programs.title: Bebras Computing Challenge
programs.summary: A short online challenge of computational thinking puzzles. No programming is needed, and there are age groups from grade 3 to 12.

programs.title: North American Computational Linguistics Open (NACLO)
programs.summary: A contest where students solve puzzles about languages and how computers process them. No prior knowledge of linguistics is needed. Top scorers can go to the International Linguistics Olympiad.
programs.when: Open round in late January; invitational round in March
programs.format: In person, At your school or a university site

programs.title: Meta Hacker Cup
programs.summary: An annual online programming contest open to anyone. It has several online rounds, and the top finalists compete for prizes.
programs.when: Usually rounds from August to October

programs.title: picoCTF
programs.summary: A free online capture-the-flag contest where students solve security puzzles in cryptography, web exploits, reverse engineering and forensics. Practice problems stay open all year.
body: Award: Prizes for top US middle and high school teams.
programs.when: Main contest usually in March; practice gym open all year

programs.title: CyberPatriot
programs.summary: A team contest where students find and fix security problems on virtual Windows and Linux computers. Teams advance through online rounds to a national final.
body: Award: Scholarships for national finalists.
Who can apply: Teams of 2 to 6 with a coach; middle and high school divisions.
programs.when: Team registration usually closes in October; rounds from fall to winter; finals in spring
programs.cost: Registration fee per team, some teams get waivers

programs.title: US Cyber Games
programs.summary: An open online capture-the-flag event followed by tryouts for the US Cyber Team, which competes in the International Cybersecurity Challenge.
body: Who can apply: US citizens; the national team has age limits.
programs.when: Open CTF usually in spring or summer; team combine after

programs.title: National Cyber League (NCL)
programs.summary: A season of online security challenges for high school and college students. It has a practice game, an individual game and a team game, with a scouting report at the end.
programs.when: Fall and spring seasons; register before each season

programs.title: US Cyber Challenge (Cyber Quests and Cyber Camps)
programs.summary: Online Cyber Quests where players analyze a security artifact and answer questions. Top scorers are invited to week-long summer Cyber Camps.
body: Who can apply: US residents 18 and older; camps need US citizenship.
programs.when: Cyber Quests in winter and spring; camps in June and July

programs.title: CSAW Capture the Flag
programs.summary: A student security contest run by NYU with an online qualifying round in September and a final round in November. It is open to high school and college students.
programs.when: Qualifying round in September; finals November 12 to 14, 2026

programs.title: HSCTF
programs.summary: A capture-the-flag contest written by high school students for high school students, with problems in cryptography, web, reverse engineering and more.
programs.when: Usually late spring or early summer

programs.title: TJCTF
programs.org: Thomas Jefferson High School for Science and Technology students
programs.summary: An online capture-the-flag contest run by TJHSST students, open to anyone, with prizes for high school teams.

programs.title: NSA Codebreaker Challenge
programs.summary: A long online challenge set from about September to January. Students work through a chain of reverse engineering and cryptography tasks based on a made-up mission.
body: Who can apply: Students at US colleges and universities.
programs.when: Opens in September; runs to January

programs.title: MITRE Embedded Capture the Flag (eCTF)
programs.summary: Teams design a secure embedded system, then try to break the other teams' designs. It runs over a semester.
programs.when: Registration in the fall; competition January to April

programs.title: National Collegiate Cyber Defense Competition (CCDC)
programs.summary: College teams run and defend a small business network while a red team attacks it. Qualifiers and regionals feed a national final.
body: Who can apply: Teams from US colleges.
programs.when: Qualifiers in winter; nationals in April

programs.title: DOE CyberForce Competition
programs.summary: A college contest where teams defend a model of an energy company's systems against attacks from a red team.
body: Who can apply: US college students.

programs.title: USA-North America AI Olympiad (USAAIO)
programs.summary: An AI contest for middle and high school students with a written part and a coding part on machine learning. Top students go on to later rounds and the team for the International Olympiad in AI.
body: Who can apply: Students in the US and Canada, under 20 and not full-time in university.
programs.when: Register by January 31, 2027; Round 1 on February 19, 2027

programs.title: International Olympiad in Artificial Intelligence (IOAI)
programs.summary: An international AI olympiad for high school students, with scientific and practical rounds on machine learning. The US team is chosen through USAAIO.
body: Award: Medals.
Who can apply: Chosen onto a national team.
programs.when: Team chosen in spring; contest in summer

programs.title: Presidential AI Challenge
programs.org: White House and partner agencies (run by ORISE)
programs.summary: Student teams build a project that uses AI to address a problem in their community, with an educator track as well. The first cycle ran in 2025-26; check the site for the next cycle.
body: Who can apply: US K-12 students with an adult advisor.
programs.when: First cycle: submissions due January 2026; next cycle not yet announced

programs.title: Wharton High School Data Science Competition
programs.org: Wharton Sports Analytics and Business Initiative
programs.summary: Teams get a sports data set and build models to make predictions, then write up their method. Past topics include ice hockey performance.
body: Who can apply: High school teams with a teacher advisor.
programs.when: Registration usually December to January; competition February to April

programs.title: Kaggle Competitions
programs.summary: Online data science contests with real data sets, from beginner practice problems to large prize contests. Students can join for free and learn from shared notebooks.
body: Who can apply: Age rules vary by contest; many prize contests require 18 or older.

programs.title: ASA Data Visualization Poster Competition
programs.summary: Students collect or find data, then make a poster with two or more graphs that answer a question. There are divisions from kindergarten to grade 12.
body: Award: Cash prizes and plaques.

programs.title: ASA DataFest
programs.summary: A weekend data analysis contest held at colleges, where undergraduate teams get a large, unseen data set and present what they find.
body: Who can apply: Undergraduates at host schools.
programs.format: In person, Host colleges in the US and abroad

programs.title: AI Mathematical Olympiad Prize (AIMO)
programs.summary: A prize fund for open AI models that can solve olympiad-level math problems. The contests run on Kaggle and anyone who meets Kaggle's rules can enter.

programs.title: COMAP Mathematical Contest in Modeling and Interdisciplinary Contest in Modeling (MCM/ICM)
programs.summary: Teams of up to three college students pick one real-world problem and have four days to build a model and write a report.
body: Award: Ratings from Successful Participant to Outstanding Winner.
Who can apply: College students with a faculty advisor.
programs.when: Registration opens in the fall; contest usually in early February

programs.title: High School Mathematical Contest in Modeling (HiMCM) and MidMCM
programs.summary: Teams of up to four students pick one open-ended problem and have a window of days to build a math model and write a solution paper. MidMCM is the middle school version.
body: Who can apply: Teams with a teacher advisor.

programs.title: MathWorks Math Modeling Challenge (M3 Challenge)
programs.summary: Teams of three to five high school juniors and seniors get 14 hours on one weekend to model a real-world problem and write a paper.
body: Award: Scholarship prizes, about $100,000 total.
Who can apply: US and UK juniors and seniors.
programs.when: Registration usually closes in February; challenge weekend in late February or early March

programs.title: International Mathematical Modeling Challenge (IMMC)
programs.summary: An international modeling contest for high school teams. US teams take part through COMAP, and top papers are sent on to the international round.
body: Who can apply: Teams of up to four with an advisor.

programs.title: Modeling the Future Challenge
programs.summary: Teams analyze data on a real risk topic and write a report with an actuarial-style model and recommendations.
body: Award: Scholarship prizes for top teams.
Who can apply: US high school students.

programs.title: Mu Alpha Theta National Convention
programs.summary: A week-long summer meeting of Mu Alpha Theta math honor society chapters, with many individual and team math tests. Chapters also run monthly national contests during the year.
body: Who can apply: Members of Mu Alpha Theta chapters.
programs.when: Registration opens March 1, 2027; convention in early summer

programs.title: Bay Area Mathematical Olympiad (BAMO)
programs.summary: A proof-based olympiad with two levels: BAMO-8 for middle school and BAMO-12 for high school. Students write full solutions to a small set of problems.
programs.when: School registration in winter; contest usually in late February
programs.format: In person, At participating schools, mostly in the San Francisco Bay Area

programs.title: MATHCOUNTS Math Video Challenge
programs.summary: Teams of four middle school students make a short video that explains a math problem and its solution with a real-world story.
body: Who can apply: Grades 6 to 8.

programs.title: Lexington Informatics Tournament (LIT)
programs.summary: An online programming contest run by high school students, with a team competitive programming round and a capture-the-flag round. Teams have up to three people.
body: Award: Cash prizes for top teams.
programs.when: Usually late July to early August

programs.title: MIT Battlecode
programs.summary: Teams write an AI player for a real-time strategy game and compete in tournaments over about a month. There are separate high school and newbie tournaments.
programs.format: Hybrid, Online, with a final event at MIT

programs.title: Cornell High School Programming Contest
programs.summary: A programming workshop and contest for high school teams held at Cornell.

programs.title: Microsoft Imagine Cup
programs.summary: A startup contest for university students who build a product using Microsoft AI and cloud tools.
body: Who can apply: University students.

programs.title: International Linguistics Olympiad (IOL)
programs.summary: An international olympiad where students solve puzzles about the structure of unfamiliar languages. The US team is chosen through NACLO.
body: Award: Medals.
Who can apply: Chosen onto the US team.
programs.when: Team chosen through NACLO in spring; contest in summer

programs.title: Advent of Code
programs.summary: A free set of daily programming puzzles in December, with two parts per puzzle. Since 2025 it runs for 12 days. Many school clubs run private leaderboards.

programs.title: Regeneron International Science and Engineering Fair (ISEF)
programs.summary: The largest international pre-college science fair. You qualify by winning at a Society-affiliated local, regional, state or national fair, then present your project to judges. ISEF 2027 is in Los Angeles in May.
body: Award: Grand awards and special awards; top awards up to $100,000.
Who can apply: Grades 9 to 12, selected by an affiliated fair.
programs.when: Qualify through an affiliated fair, usually January to April

programs.title: ISEF-affiliated regional and state science fairs
programs.summary: Hundreds of local, regional and state fairs around the world are affiliated with ISEF. You enter your research project at your local fair, and top projects move on to ISEF (high school) or can be nominated to Thermo Fisher JIC (middle school).
body: Who can apply: Depends on the fair; usually based on where you live or go to school.
programs.when: Varies by fair, usually winter to early spring

programs.title: Thermo Fisher Scientific Junior Innovators Challenge (JIC)
programs.summary: The national research competition for middle school students. The top 10% of 6th to 8th graders at affiliated fairs can be nominated, then apply online; 30 finalists go to Washington, DC in October.
body: Award: Top award $25,000.
Who can apply: US students in grades 6 to 8, nominated by an affiliated fair.
programs.when: Usually February to early June (after nomination)

programs.title: Junior Science and Humanities Symposium (JSHS)
programs.org: Department of War (Army, Navy, Air Force), run by NSTA
programs.summary: High school students present original research as a talk or poster at one of about 48 regional symposia. The top five from each region go to the National JSHS in the spring.
body: Award: Undergraduate tuition scholarships at regional and national level.
Who can apply: Grades 9 to 12, US citizens or permanent residents.
programs.when: Regional deadlines vary, symposia usually January to March

programs.title: GENIUS Olympiad
programs.org: Terra Science and Education, hosted by St. John Fisher University
programs.summary: An international project fair about environmental issues, with categories in science, engineering, business, art, writing, music, film, speech and coding. Finalists present in Rochester, New York in June.
body: Who can apply: Grades 8 to 12 worldwide.

programs.title: Stockholm Junior Water Prize (US)
programs.summary: A research competition for water-related science projects. You enter through your state competition; the US winner goes to Stockholm to compete for the international prize.
body: Award: US winner goes to the international final in Stockholm.
Who can apply: Grades 9 to 12, age 15 by August 1; teams of up to two.
programs.when: State entry usually mid-April; national paper due in May

programs.title: USA Biology Olympiad (USABO)
programs.summary: A biology exam series held at your school. The Open Exam in February leads to a Semifinal, then about 20 finalists go to a two-week camp that picks four students for the International Biology Olympiad.
body: Award: Medals; path to the International Biology Olympiad team.
Who can apply: US high school students; school must register as a test site.
programs.when: School registration in fall; Open Exam usually early February
programs.format: In person, At your school, then a national camp

programs.title: US National Chemistry Olympiad (USNCO)
programs.summary: A chemistry contest that starts with a local exam run by your ACS local section in March. Top scorers take the national exam in April, and about 20 go to a study camp that picks the four-person team for the International Chemistry Olympiad.
body: Award: Path to the International Chemistry Olympiad team.
Who can apply: US high school students, chosen by their ACS local section.
programs.when: Local section exams usually March; national exam April
programs.format: In person, At a local testing site

programs.title: Physics Olympiad: F=ma exam
programs.summary: A 75-minute, 25-question mechanics exam taken at your school. It is the first step toward the US Physics Team.
body: Award: Qualifies top scorers for USAPhO.
Who can apply: US high school students; a teacher registers the school.
programs.when: Register by December; exam usually late January or early February

programs.title: USA Physics Olympiad (USAPhO)
programs.summary: A free-response physics exam for the top F=ma scorers. The top 20 or so go to the US Physics Team training camp, which picks five students for the International Physics Olympiad.
body: Award: Medals; path to the International Physics Olympiad team.
Who can apply: Invited based on F=ma score.
programs.when: By invitation after F=ma; exam usually in spring

programs.title: PhysicsBowl
programs.summary: A 40-question, 45-minute multiple-choice physics exam taken at your school. There are divisions for first-year and second-year physics students, and schools are ranked by region.
body: Who can apply: High school students; a teacher registers.
programs.when: Registration opens in December; deadline usually late February

programs.title: USA Earth Science Olympiad (USESO)
programs.summary: A national Earth science exam in March, followed by a week-long training camp in June. The camp picks the US team for the International Earth Science Olympiad.
body: Award: Path to the International Earth Science Olympiad team.
Who can apply: US high school students.
programs.when: Registration usually opens around December; exam in March

programs.title: USA Astronomy and Astrophysics Olympiad (USAAAO)
programs.summary: An online astronomy exam in February, then a harder National Astronomy Competition in April. Top students train over the summer, and the team goes to the International Olympiad on Astronomy and Astrophysics.
body: Award: Path to the IOAA team.
Who can apply: US high school students; needs a proctor.
programs.when: Registration usually January 1 to 31; first round in February
programs.cost: $30 per student, $20 with 5 or more from one school; aid available

programs.title: Brain Bee
programs.summary: A neuroscience competition for teens. You compete in a local Brain Bee, then a national championship, and each country's winner goes to the International Brain Bee World Championship.
body: Who can apply: Ages 13 to 19, through a local chapter.
programs.when: Local chapters usually run in winter and spring

programs.title: Physics Cup
programs.summary: An online physics problem contest. A hard problem is posted about every two weeks from October to February, and you send in your solutions.
body: Who can apply: High school students worldwide.

programs.title: International Young Physicists' Tournament (IYPT)
programs.summary: Teams of five spend months on 17 open-ended physics problems, then defend their solutions against other teams in debate-style rounds. IYPT 2027 is in Auckland, New Zealand in July.
body: Who can apply: High school teams selected by their country.
programs.when: Problems published in July; national selection varies by country

programs.title: Science Olympiad
programs.summary: Teams of up to 15 compete in 23 events covering biology, chemistry, physics, earth science and engineering builds. Teams go from regional to state tournaments, and the best go to the national tournament in May.
body: Who can apply: Division B (grades 6 to 9) and Division C (grades 9 to 12); some states run Division A for elementary.
programs.when: Join through your state chapter in fall; tournaments January to May

programs.title: National Science Bowl
programs.summary: A fast buzzer quiz in biology, chemistry, earth and space science, energy, math and physics. Teams of four or five win a regional bowl to go to the National Finals in Washington, DC, held April 29 to May 3, 2027. Middle schools also build and race a car.
body: Award: Prize money for school science departments at nationals.
Who can apply: Teams from one school, grades 6 to 8 or 9 to 12.
programs.when: Regional registration usually in fall; regionals January to March

programs.title: National Ocean Sciences Bowl (NOSB)
programs.summary: A quiz bowl about ocean science. Teams of four or five compete at regional bowls, with a virtual option in March 2027 and a national finals round.
body: Who can apply: High school teams from one school.
programs.when: Regional bowls usually February to March

programs.title: CEF You Be The Solution Challenge
programs.org: CEF in STEM (formerly Chemical Educational Foundation)
programs.summary: The program formerly called You Be The Chemist Challenge. Teams of three or four answer timed science questions at a regional event and make a short video on a real problem; the top 10 teams go to the national event in Houston.
body: Award: Scholarships at national level.
Who can apply: Grades 5 to 8.

programs.title: TEAMS (Tests of Engineering Aptitude, Mathematics, and Science)
programs.summary: Teams of four to six take a timed engineering and science test and do a design and build task at a state event in January or February. Top teams nationally go to the TEAMS national competition in Orlando in June 2027.
body: Who can apply: Middle and high school teams; TSA membership not required.
programs.when: State competitions usually January to February

programs.title: FIRST LEGO League
programs.summary: Teams build and program LEGO robots for a table game and do a research project on a yearly theme. The Challenge division competes at qualifiers and state events; Discover and Explore are for younger kids.
body: Who can apply: Ages 4 to 16 (grades K to 8 in the US).
programs.when: Registration usually August to fall; events November to March

programs.title: FIRST Tech Challenge
programs.summary: Teams of up to 15 design, build and program a mid-size robot for a new game each fall. Teams play at league and qualifying events, then state championships and the FIRST Championship.
body: Award: Awards and access to FIRST scholarships.
Who can apply: Grades 7 to 12.
programs.when: Registration usually opens in spring and summer; season September to April
programs.cost: Team registration and parts fees; grants available

programs.title: FIRST Robotics Competition
programs.summary: High school teams get a new game in January and have about six weeks to build a large robot. They play at district or regional events in spring, and the best go to the FIRST Championship in April.
body: Award: Awards and access to FIRST scholarships.
Who can apply: Grades 9 to 12.
programs.when: Registration usually fall; kickoff in early January

programs.title: VEX IQ Robotics Competition
programs.summary: Teams build a small snap-together VEX IQ robot for a yearly game and also compete in driving and autonomous skills. Events lead to state championships and the VEX Robotics World Championship.
body: Who can apply: Elementary and middle school students.
programs.when: Season runs roughly May to April; events mostly fall to spring
programs.cost: Team registration and robot kit fees

programs.title: VEX V5 Robotics Competition
programs.summary: Teams build a metal VEX V5 robot for a new game each year and compete in matches and skills runs at local tournaments. Top teams go on to state or regional championships and the VEX Robotics World Championship.
body: Who can apply: Middle and high school students.
programs.when: Season runs roughly May to April; events mostly fall to spring
programs.cost: Team registration and robot kit fees

programs.title: VEX U and VEX AI
programs.summary: College teams build VEX robots with fewer part limits and custom parts, and VEX AI teams build fully autonomous robots. Both play the yearly game and compete at the VEX Robotics World Championship.
body: Who can apply: College teams (VEX U); high school and college teams (VEX AI).
programs.when: Season runs roughly May to April

programs.title: BEST Robotics
programs.summary: Teams get a kit of basic materials and six to eight weeks to build a robot for a new game. Hubs hold a game day in fall, and winners go to regional championships.
body: Who can apply: Middle and high school teams.
programs.when: Registration in summer; kickoff usually September, game day October to November
programs.cost: Hubs supply the kit of materials

programs.title: Botball
programs.summary: Teams get a kit and build and program fully autonomous robots, with no remote control, for a tournament game. There are regional tournaments in spring and an international tournament in summer.
body: Who can apply: Middle and high school teams.
programs.when: Registration usually fall to winter; tournaments spring
programs.cost: Team registration includes a robot kit

programs.title: RoboCupJunior
programs.summary: Students build autonomous robots for soccer, rescue or onstage challenges. There are local and regional events and an international RoboCupJunior event held with the RoboCup world championship.
body: Who can apply: Students up to age 19.

programs.title: World Robot Olympiad (WRO)
programs.summary: An international robotics competition with categories for robot missions, future innovators projects, robot sports and future engineers self-driving cars. Countries hold national rounds, and winners go to the international final in November.
body: Who can apply: Ages 8 to 22, depending on category.
programs.when: National rounds usually spring to summer

programs.title: SeaPerch
programs.summary: Students build a small underwater robot (ROV) from a kit and run it through obstacle and mission courses in a pool. Regional events lead to the International SeaPerch Challenge, held June 5 to 6, 2027.
body: Who can apply: Elementary, middle and high school teams.
programs.when: Regional events usually February to April

programs.title: MATE ROV Competition
programs.org: Marine Advanced Technology Education (MATE) Inspiration for Innovation
programs.summary: Teams design and build underwater robots to do tasks based on real ocean jobs, and write a technical report and give a presentation. There are several classes by experience level, from beginner regional classes to the world championship classes.
body: Who can apply: Middle school through college, by class.
programs.when: Regional contests usually spring; world championship in summer

programs.title: RoboSub
programs.summary: Teams build fully autonomous underwater vehicles that must find and complete tasks in a pool without a driver. The event is held once a year in late July or early August.
body: Who can apply: High school, undergraduate and graduate teams.
programs.when: Usually register in winter; competition late July or early August

programs.title: RoboBoat
programs.summary: Teams build autonomous surface boats that navigate a course and complete tasks on their own. It runs once a year.
body: Who can apply: High school and college teams.
programs.when: Usually register in fall to winter; event in spring

programs.title: Zero Robotics
programs.summary: Students write code to control satellites in a simulated game. The middle school program runs in the summer and finals are held online.
body: Who can apply: Middle school students, usually through a summer program.

programs.title: American Rocketry Challenge
programs.org: Aerospace Industries Association and National Association of Rocketry
programs.summary: Teams design, build and fly a model rocket that must hit a target altitude and flight time while carrying an egg. The top 100 teams go to the national finals, and the winner flies at an international competition.
body: Who can apply: Grades 6 to 12, US teams of 3 to 10.
programs.cost: Team registration fee plus rocket parts

programs.title: NASA Student Launch
programs.summary: Teams spend a school year designing, building and launching a high-power rocket with a science or engineering payload, with NASA design reviews along the way. The final launch is in Huntsville, Alabama on April 10, 2027.
body: Who can apply: US colleges and qualifying grade 6 to 12 teams.
programs.when: Proposals usually due in late summer or early fall

programs.title: NASA Human Exploration Rover Challenge (HERC)
programs.summary: Teams design and build a human-powered rover and drive it through an obstacle course with mission tasks. The 2027 event is April 21 to 24 at the US Space and Rocket Center.
body: Who can apply: US and international teams, grades 6 to 12 and college.
programs.when: Proposals usually due in September (September 17, 2026 this cycle)

programs.title: NASA TechRise Student Challenge
programs.summary: Student teams write a proposal for an experiment to fly on a high-altitude balloon or suborbital rocket. Sixty winning teams get $1,500 and a kit to build it, and the experiments fly in summer 2027.
body: Award: $1,500 build budget and a flight test.
Who can apply: Grades 6 to 12 at US schools; teams of 4 or more with an educator.

programs.title: NASA HUNCH (High Schools United with NASA to Create Hardware)
programs.summary: High school classes design and build real products for NASA, such as items for the International Space Station, and also run design, video and culinary challenges. Top students present their work at a NASA center in spring.
body: Who can apply: High schools that join the program.
programs.when: School registration usually August to November

programs.title: Cubes in Space
programs.summary: Students design a small experiment that fits in a 4 cm or 10 cm cube. Selected experiments fly on a NASA sounding rocket or scientific balloon in summer and are returned to the students.
body: Who can apply: Ages 11 to 18, through an educator.
programs.when: Registration opens November 9, 2026; proposals usually due in winter

programs.title: Student Spaceflight Experiments Program (SSEP)
programs.org: National Center for Earth and Space Science Education
programs.summary: Students across a school community propose microgravity experiments, and one is picked to fly to the International Space Station. Communities must sign up and pay for a flight slot.
body: Who can apply: Schools and communities that join a mission.
programs.cost: Community pays a program fee, often through local sponsors

programs.title: Genes in Space
programs.summary: Students propose a DNA experiment to run in space. Finalists get mentors and present at a conference, and the winning experiment is run on the International Space Station.
body: Award: Winning experiment flies to the ISS.
Who can apply: Grades 7 to 12 in the US.
programs.when: Competition opens in January; deadline usually April

programs.title: NASA Lunabotics
programs.summary: College teams design and build a robot that digs and builds a berm in lunar-like soil, working toward construction on the Moon. The 2027 challenge is May 24 to 27 at Kennedy Space Center.
body: Who can apply: US colleges and technical schools.
programs.when: Project plan usually due in early October (October 6, 2026)
programs.format: In person, Kennedy Space Center, Florida

programs.title: Micro-g Neutral Buoyancy Experiment Design Teams (Micro-g NExT)
programs.summary: College teams design and build a tool for a spacewalk-style task. Selected teams test it in NASA's Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory pool, run by divers, from June 6 to 9, 2027.
body: Who can apply: US college students.
programs.format: In person, Johnson Space Center, Houston

programs.title: NASA SUITS (Spacesuit User Interface Technologies for Students)
programs.summary: College teams build a heads-up display or other interface to help astronauts on a Moon or Mars mission. Selected teams test their designs at Johnson Space Center, May 16 to 20, 2027.
body: Who can apply: US citizen and permanent resident college students.
programs.when: Proposal window opens late August; due in fall
programs.format: In person, Johnson Space Center, Houston

programs.title: CanSat Competition
programs.summary: College teams build a small satellite-like payload that is launched by rocket and must descend, collect data and send it to the ground. The 2027 launch is June 10 to 13 in Virginia.
body: Who can apply: College teams worldwide.
programs.cost: Teams pay for construction and travel

programs.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge
programs.summary: A two-day global hackathon where teams use NASA data to solve challenges about Earth and space. You join a local event or compete online; the 2026 event is November 14 to 15.
body: Who can apply: Open to all ages; minors need a parent's consent.

programs.title: NASA Dream With Us Design Challenge
programs.summary: A yearly aviation design challenge with a middle school design track and a high school engineering track. The 2026-27 theme is new energy systems for flight, and students submit a design and an engineering notebook.
body: Who can apply: US middle and high school students.
programs.when: Opens September 25, 2026; entries due in spring

programs.title: Future City Competition
programs.summary: Teams imagine and design a city 100 years in the future that solves a yearly problem. They build it in SimCity, write an essay, build a scale model and present to judges at a regional event in January, with finals in February.
body: Who can apply: Middle school division and high school division.
programs.when: Registration usually fall; projects due around January

programs.title: Technology Student Association (TSA) competitions
programs.summary: TSA chapters compete in more than 60 events, including engineering design, coding, biotechnology, robotics, flight and video. Students compete at state conferences in spring and the national conference in summer.
body: Who can apply: Members of a school TSA chapter.
programs.when: State conferences usually February to April

programs.title: SkillsUSA Championships
programs.summary: Career and technical students compete in more than 100 contests, including robotics and automation, engineering technology, drone work and electronics. Local and state contests lead to the national championships in June.
body: Who can apply: SkillsUSA members in career and technical programs.

programs.title: International Genetically Engineered Machine (iGEM) Competition
programs.summary: Teams spend months on a synthetic biology project, running lab work and building a website and presentation. They present at the Grand Jamboree in Paris in the fall. There are high school, undergraduate and overgraduate divisions.
body: Who can apply: High school and university teams worldwide.
programs.cost: Team registration fee plus lab and travel costs

programs.title: Formula SAE
programs.summary: College teams design, build and race a small formula-style race car. They are judged on design, cost and business presentations as well as on-track events.
body: Who can apply: College teams.
programs.when: Registration usually opens in fall; competitions in spring and summer

programs.title: Baja SAE
programs.summary: College teams design and build a single-seat off-road vehicle that races through rough terrain. Events include design judging, hill climbs and a four-hour endurance race.
body: Who can apply: College teams.
programs.when: Registration usually opens in fall; competitions in spring

programs.title: ASCE Concrete Canoe Competition
programs.summary: College civil engineering teams design and build a canoe made of concrete, write a technical report and race it. Top teams from student symposia go to the Civil Engineering Student Championships, June 17 to 19, 2027 at Kansas State University.
body: Who can apply: ASCE student chapters.

programs.title: AIAA Design/Build/Fly
programs.org: American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics
programs.summary: College teams design, build and fly a radio-controlled aircraft for a new mission each year. Teams submit a proposal and a design report, and the fly-off is April 15 to 18, 2027 in Tucson, Arizona.
body: Who can apply: College teams.
programs.when: Proposals due in fall (window opens October 15, 2026)

programs.title: Shell Eco-marathon
programs.summary: Student teams design and build ultra-efficient vehicles and compete to go farthest on the least energy. There are regional events, including one for the Americas.
body: Who can apply: High school and college teams.

programs.title: Solar Car Challenge
programs.summary: High school teams spend a year or more designing and building a road-worthy solar-powered car. They race it in a multi-day event, usually in Texas in July.
body: Who can apply: High school teams.
programs.when: Registration usually in fall; race in summer

programs.title: Greenpower USA
programs.summary: Teams build a small electric race car from a kit (Goblin for grades 4 to 6) or a larger single-seat car (F24 for grades 6 to 12), then race it at events during the school year.
body: Who can apply: Grades 4 to 12.
programs.when: Season schedule published in late summer

programs.title: Electrathon America
programs.summary: Teams design, build and race single-seat electric vehicles with a fixed battery. The goal is to go the farthest in one hour. There are high school and open divisions.
body: Who can apply: High school division plus open division.
programs.when: Races through the season; register for the season

programs.title: Destination Imagination
programs.summary: Teams pick one of six challenges, several of them engineering or technical, and spend months building a solution they present at a tournament. Tournaments go from regional to state to Global Finals in May.
body: Who can apply: Grades 3 to 12 and university.
programs.when: Team registration usually fall; tournaments February to May

programs.title: Odyssey of the Mind
programs.summary: Teams of up to seven solve a long-term problem, some of which call for building vehicles or structures, and present it within a cost limit. They also solve a surprise problem on the day. Winners go from regional to state to the World Finals.
body: Who can apply: Kindergarten through college.
programs.when: Membership usually fall; tournaments February to April

programs.title: 3M Young Scientist Challenge
programs.summary: You make a one to two minute video about a new idea to solve an everyday problem. Ten finalists get a summer mentorship with a 3M scientist and compete in October for the top prize.
body: Award: Grand prize $25,000; finalists $1,000.
Who can apply: US students in grades 5 to 8.
programs.when: Usually opens in January; closes around late April

programs.title: Toshiba/NSTA ExploraVision
programs.org: Toshiba America and National Science Teaching Association
programs.summary: Teams of two to four imagine a technology that could exist 10 or more years from now, research the science behind it and write a report with a coach. Regional winners make a website, and national winners go to an awards event.
body: Award: Savings bonds for national and regional winners.
Who can apply: US and Canadian students, grades K to 12, teams with a teacher coach.
programs.when: Usually late January or early February

programs.title: Samsung Solve for Tomorrow
programs.summary: Teacher-led student teams use STEM to solve a problem in their community. Schools move from state to national rounds, and winning schools get technology and classroom resources. The 2026-27 contest launches September 30.
body: Award: Up to $50,000 in prizes for the school.
Who can apply: US public school teachers and their grade 6 to 12 students.
programs.when: Opens September 30, 2026; first entries usually due in fall

programs.title: eCYBERMISSION
programs.org: US Army Educational Outreach Program, run by NSTA
programs.summary: Teams of two to four pick a problem in their community and investigate it with science or solve it with engineering, then submit an online Mission Folder. Winners go from state to regional to national.
body: Award: Savings bonds: $1,000 state, up to $10,000 national per student at maturity.
Who can apply: Grades 6 to 9 in the US, with an adult Team Advisor.
programs.when: Registration closes February 24, 2027; Mission Folders due March 3, 2027

programs.title: Breakthrough Junior Challenge
programs.summary: You make a short video of up to three minutes that explains a hard idea in physics, life sciences or math. Videos are peer-reviewed, then judged, and one winner is picked worldwide.
body: Award: $250,000 scholarship; $50,000 for your teacher; $100,000 science lab for your school.
Who can apply: Ages 13 to 18 worldwide.

programs.title: Lemelson-MIT InvenTeams
programs.summary: High school teams of students, teachers and mentors get a grant to spend a school year inventing a technology to solve a real problem. They present the prototype at a year-end event.
body: Award: $7,500 grant per team.
Who can apply: US high school teams.
programs.when: Application timing varies; check the site

programs.title: Invention Convention Worldwide
programs.summary: Students find a problem, invent a solution, build a prototype and present it with a logbook. Local and state affiliate events lead to Invention Convention US Nationals in Dearborn, Michigan in spring.
body: Who can apply: Grades K to 12 through a local affiliate.
programs.when: Local events usually winter to spring

programs.title: NCF-Envirothon
programs.summary: Teams of five take hands-on field tests in soils, forestry, aquatic ecology, wildlife and a yearly current issue, and give an oral presentation. State winners go to the international competition, July 24 to 30, 2027 in Maryland.
body: Who can apply: Grades 9 to 12 or ages 14 to 19.

programs.title: The Earth Prize
programs.summary: A global sustainability competition where student teams design a solution to an environmental problem and submit a proposal. Registrations for 2027 are open.
body: Who can apply: Ages 13 to 19 worldwide, in teams with a mentor.
programs.when: Registration usually fall; submissions in winter

programs.title: President's Environmental Youth Award
programs.summary: Students run an environmental project in their community and apply with an adult sponsor. EPA can choose one winner from each of its ten regions in two categories.
body: Award: Presidential plaque.
Who can apply: Grades K to 5 and 6 to 12 in the US.
programs.when: Varies by year; check the EPA page

programs.title: Gloria Barron Prize for Young Heroes
programs.summary: An award for young people who led a project that helps people or the environment. Many past winners ran conservation or science-based projects.
body: Who can apply: Ages 8 to 18 in the US and Canada.

programs.title: Research Science Institute (RSI)
programs.org: Center for Excellence in Education and MIT
programs.summary: Six weeks at MIT: one week of classes, five weeks of research with a mentor, then presentations. Students apply in 11th grade and must be 16 by July 1. Very selective.
body: The 2027 dates are not posted yet. The deadline follows a fixed rule, the Wednesday of the second full week of December, so it should be close.
programs.when: Applications due in December of junior year

programs.title: PROMYS
programs.summary: A six-week residential math program built around number theory. The application includes a set of problems to work on. Students must have finished 9th grade and be 14 to 18 when the program starts.
programs.when: Applications due at the end of February
programs.cost: Up to $8,000. Free for families earning under $80,000, with aid above that

programs.title: Ross Mathematics Program
programs.summary: A six-week summer program built around number theory. Students work through problem sets that ask them to prove things on their own, with help from counselors.
body: Who can apply: Pre-college students, roughly ages 15 to 18.

programs.title: PROMYS Europe
programs.summary: A European version of PROMYS held at the University of Oxford. Six weeks of number theory problem sets, lectures and seminars.
body: Who can apply: Pre-university students, mainly from Europe.
programs.when: Usually early spring, with application problems

programs.title: Hampshire College Summer Studies in Mathematics (HCSSiM)
programs.summary: A six-week residential math program. Students take workshop classes in proof-based topics and do daily problem sets and short projects.

programs.title: Canada/USA Mathcamp
programs.summary: A five-week residential camp where students choose from many classes in higher math taught by mathematicians and college students. Admission is based on a Qualifying Quiz of hard problems.
body: Who can apply: Ages 13 to 18.
programs.format: In person, A college campus in North America, changes yearly

programs.title: Stanford University Mathematics Camp (SUMaC)
programs.summary: An online summer program in advanced math such as abstract algebra and number theory. Students attend live classes, do daily problem sets and finish a group research project.
body: Who can apply: Students in grades 10 and 11.

programs.title: MathILy
programs.summary: A five-week residential program in college-level discrete math and proofs. Students take intensive root classes and then choose shorter topic classes.
programs.format: In person, Bryn Mawr College, PA

programs.title: Texas State Honors Summer Math Camp
programs.summary: A six-week residential camp. Students take a proof-based number theory course and later work on small research projects.
body: Who can apply: Students ages 15 and older.

programs.title: AwesomeMath Summer Program
programs.summary: A three-week summer program in competition math. Students take courses at their level on problem solving for contests like the AMC, AIME and olympiads.

programs.title: Idea Math Summer Program
programs.summary: Summer classes in competition math and problem solving for middle and high school students. Classes are sorted by level and aimed at contests like MATHCOUNTS and AMC.

programs.title: MathPath
programs.summary: A four-week residential summer camp for younger students who love math. Campers take math classes in the morning and do problem solving and activities in the afternoon.
body: Who can apply: Ages 11 to 14.
programs.when: Usually spring, with a qualifying test

programs.title: Epsilon Camp
programs.summary: A two-week residential math camp for very young, mathematically gifted children. Campers take courses in topics like number theory and logic, and a parent stays nearby.
body: Who can apply: Ages 7 to 12.

programs.title: BEAM (Bridge to Enter Advanced Mathematics)
programs.summary: A free program for middle school students from low-income communities. It starts with a summer math program and then supports students with classes and advising through high school.
body: Who can apply: Students from low-income communities, starting in grades 6 to 7.
programs.format: In person, New York City and Los Angeles

programs.title: Summer Program in Mathematical Problem Solving (SPMPS)
programs.summary: A free three-week residential math camp for seventh graders from low-income families in New York City. Students work on problem solving and proofs in small classes.
body: Who can apply: NYC seventh graders from low-income backgrounds.
programs.format: In person, Bard College, NY, with bus from NYC

programs.title: All Girls/All Math
programs.summary: A week-long summer math camp for girls. Campers take a course in an advanced topic, meet women in math and live on campus.
body: Who can apply: Girls entering grades 10 to 12 who have finished geometry.

programs.title: UChicago Young Scholars Program
programs.org: University of Chicago, Department of Mathematics
programs.summary: A selective four-week summer day camp in math for Chicago-area students. Students study topics not usually taught in school.
body: Who can apply: Chicago-area students entering grades 7 to 12.

programs.title: MIT Math ROOTS
programs.summary: A free two-week residential summer program at MIT in creative math and problem solving. It is aimed at high-potential students from underrepresented backgrounds.
body: Who can apply: High school students, ages 14 to 18.

programs.title: SigmaCamp
programs.summary: A one-week sleepaway camp in math and science run by volunteer scientists. Campers pick a small research-style project and attend lectures. SigmaNext and SigmaWest are sister camps.
body: Who can apply: Ages 12 to 17.

programs.title: Euler Circle
programs.summary: College-level math classes for advanced high school students, including a research track where students write a paper. Classes run during the school year and in summer.
programs.format: Hybrid, Palo Alto, CA, and online

programs.title: Girls Talk Math
programs.summary: A free summer day camp for high school girls and gender minorities. Campers work on math problem sets and make blog posts and podcasts about math.

programs.title: Simons Summer Research Program
programs.summary: A seven-week summer program where students do research in a Stony Brook lab with a faculty mentor. It ends with a written abstract and a poster symposium.
body: Who can apply: High school juniors, US citizens or permanent residents.

programs.title: Anson L. Clark Scholars Program
programs.summary: A seven-week summer research program for 12 students. Each scholar works on a research project with a Texas Tech faculty member and writes a report.
body: Who can apply: Rising seniors and recent graduates, age 17 by the start.
programs.cost: Free, housing and meals included; $750 stipend

programs.title: Summer Science Program (SSP)
programs.summary: A residential research program where teams of three do a real research project, such as finding the orbit of an asteroid or studying an enzyme. Programs run in astrophysics, biochemistry and genomics.
body: Who can apply: Mainly high school juniors.
programs.cost: Tuition, need-based aid up to full cost
programs.format: In person, Several US university campuses

programs.title: Research in Science and Engineering (RISE)
programs.summary: A six-week summer program for rising seniors. Students either join a BU lab for a research internship or take the practicum track, and present at a poster symposium.
body: Who can apply: High school juniors who are US citizens or residents.

programs.title: Summer Science Research Program (SSRP)
programs.summary: A seven-week lab research program in New York City. Students learn lab skills, then work on their own question with a small team and present at a symposium.
body: Who can apply: High school juniors and seniors, age 16 or older.

programs.title: Garcia Summer Research Program
programs.org: Stony Brook University, Garcia Center for Polymers at Engineered Interfaces
programs.summary: A seven-week summer program in materials science and polymer research. Students work in a lab on a project and many submit their work to science competitions.

programs.title: Research Mentorship Program (RMP)
programs.summary: A six-week summer program where students do an interdisciplinary research project with a UCSB mentor. Students take classes on research and present at a symposium.
body: Who can apply: Students in grades 10 and 11.
programs.format: Hybrid, Santa Barbara, CA, or online

programs.title: Secondary Student Training Program (SSTP)
programs.summary: A 5.5-week summer research program. Students live on campus and work in a university lab with a faculty mentor, then present their research.
body: Who can apply: Students in grades 10 and 11.

programs.title: Young Scholars Program (YSP)
programs.summary: A six-week residential science and math program. Students take classes and work on a research project with an FSU faculty member.
body: Who can apply: Florida high school students who have finished grade 11.

programs.title: ARISE (Applied Research Innovations in Science and Engineering)
programs.summary: A free 10-week summer program for New York City students. Students first take workshops, then do research in an NYU lab and receive a stipend when they finish.
body: Who can apply: NYC high school sophomores and juniors.

programs.title: Stanford Institutes of Medicine Summer Research Program (SIMR)
programs.summary: An eight-week summer program where students do biomedical research in a Stanford lab with a mentor. It ends with a poster session.
body: Who can apply: High school juniors and seniors, age 16 or older, US citizens or permanent residents.

programs.title: SHTEM: Summer Internships for High Schoolers
programs.summary: An eight-week summer research program where small teams work on projects that mix science, engineering and the humanities, with Stanford mentors.
body: Who can apply: High school juniors and seniors, US citizens or permanent residents.

programs.title: JAX Summer Student Program
programs.summary: A 10-week paid summer research program in genetics and genomics. Each student runs an independent project with a JAX scientist and presents it at the end.
body: Who can apply: High school students who have finished grade 11, and undergraduates.
programs.cost: Paid stipend, room and board included
programs.format: In person, Bar Harbor, ME (high school students)

programs.title: Summer High School Internship Program (SHIP)
programs.summary: An eight-week paid internship. Students get two weeks of lab training, then spend six weeks in a Fred Hutch research group.
body: Who can apply: Students between grades 11 and 12, Washington state.
programs.when: Info usually posted in November; apply in winter

programs.title: Laboratory Learning Program (LLP)
programs.summary: A free summer program where students join ongoing research in a Princeton science or engineering lab for five to six weeks.
body: Who can apply: New Jersey high school students, age 16 or older, US citizens.

programs.title: COSMOS (California State Summer School for Mathematics and Science)
programs.summary: A four-week residential program at several UC campuses. Students join a cluster on one topic, take classes, work in labs and finish a team project.
body: Who can apply: California students in grades 8 to 12.
programs.format: In person, UC Davis, Irvine, Merced, San Diego, Santa Cruz

programs.title: Science Internship Program (SIP)
programs.summary: An eight-week research program. Small groups of students work on a project with a UCSC mentor in fields like astronomy, computer science and environmental science, then present a poster.
body: Who can apply: Students ages 14 to 17.
programs.cost: Tuition, need-based aid up to full cost

programs.title: Aspiring Scientists Summer Internship Program (ASSIP)
programs.summary: An eight-week research internship where each student works with a George Mason faculty mentor and earns college credit. It ends with a research presentation.
body: Who can apply: High school students and undergraduates.
programs.cost: Tuition for credit, waivers for need
programs.format: Hybrid, Fairfax and Manassas, VA, or online

programs.title: Student Science Training Program (UF SSTP)
programs.summary: A seven-week residential research program. Students work 30 hours a week in a faculty lab, attend lectures, write a research paper and present a poster.
body: Who can apply: Rising seniors age 16 or older.
programs.cost: Tuition, limited aid for Florida students

programs.title: Waksman Institute Summer Experience (WISE)
programs.summary: A two-week summer program in molecular biology and bioinformatics. Students generate and study new DNA sequences and can have their results published in GenBank.

programs.title: MIT THINK Scholars Program
programs.summary: High school students send a proposal for a science, technology or engineering project. A few finalists get funding, weekly mentoring from MIT students, and a trip to MIT.
body: Award: Up to $1,000 in project funding, trip to MIT.
Who can apply: US high school students.

programs.title: Wolfram Summer Research Program
programs.summary: A summer program where each student completes a research project in computation, math or science using the Wolfram Language, with a mentor.
programs.format: In person, Bentley University, Waltham, MA

programs.title: Mathworks Junior Summer Math Camp
programs.summary: A summer math camp for younger students, with half-day and residential versions. Students work on problem solving and early proof-based math.

programs.title: Girls' Angle
programs.summary: A math club for girls that meets weekly during the school year. Members work with women mentors on math at their own level and pace.

programs.title: Research in the Biological Sciences (RIBS)
programs.summary: A four-week lab course for high school students. Students learn molecular and cell biology techniques, run a project and present the results at a research forum.

programs.title: Summer@ICERM
programs.summary: An eight-week residential math research program for undergraduates. Students work in small groups on problems in pure and applied math with faculty advisors.
body: Who can apply: Current undergraduates.

programs.title: Research Experiences for Undergraduates (REU)
programs.summary: NSF funds hundreds of summer research sites at universities in almost every science field. Undergraduates apply to each site and do a research project with faculty, usually for 8 to 10 weeks.
body: Who can apply: Undergraduates who are US citizens or permanent residents.
programs.when: Usually February to March, varies by site
programs.format: In person, Universities across the US

programs.title: MIT Beaver Works Summer Institute (BWSI)
programs.summary: A four-week summer program at MIT for rising seniors, with project-based courses in topics like autonomous vehicles, AI, radar and satellites. Students do an online course first as part of applying.
body: Who can apply: Rising high school seniors.

programs.title: MIT Women's Technology Program (WTP)
programs.summary: A free four-week summer program at MIT that introduces engineering through classes, labs and team projects. It is for students with strong math and science grades and little prior engineering background.
body: Who can apply: Rising high school seniors.

programs.title: MITES Summer
programs.org: MIT Introduction to Technology, Engineering, and Science (MITES)
programs.summary: A free six-week residential program at MIT where students take college-level math, science and humanities courses. Travel scholarships are available.
body: Who can apply: Rising high school seniors.

programs.title: MITES Semester
programs.org: MIT Introduction to Technology, Engineering, and Science (MITES)
programs.summary: A free six-month online program, June to December, for rising seniors. Students take courses in STEM topics and get college admissions help.
body: Who can apply: Rising high school seniors.

programs.title: Summer Academy for Math and Science (SAMS)
programs.summary: A merit-based summer program at Carnegie Mellon in math, science and engineering, with classes and a team project. Admitted students pay no tuition.
body: Who can apply: Rising high school juniors and seniors.
programs.format: In person, Carnegie Mellon, Pittsburgh, PA

programs.title: CMU AI Scholars
programs.summary: A fully funded four-week residential program in AI for rising seniors. Students take classes, do group projects and present at a final symposium.
body: Who can apply: Rising high school seniors.
programs.format: In person, Carnegie Mellon, Pittsburgh, PA

programs.title: CMU CS Scholars
programs.summary: A fully funded four-week residential program in computer science for rising sophomores, with classes, projects, faculty talks and visits from tech companies.
body: Who can apply: Rising high school sophomores.
programs.format: In person, Carnegie Mellon, Pittsburgh, PA

programs.title: Kode With Klossy Camp
programs.summary: Free two-week summer coding camps, online or in person in several cities, in areas like data science, machine learning and AI. For young women and gender-expansive teens.
body: Who can apply: Ages 13 to 18.

programs.title: Girls Who Code Pathways
programs.summary: A free, self-paced virtual coding program for high school students. Girls Who Code also runs free after-school clubs for grades 3 to 12.
body: Who can apply: High school students.

programs.title: Engineering Summer Academy at Penn (ESAP)
programs.org: University of Pennsylvania School of Engineering and Applied Science
programs.summary: A three-week summer program at Penn with tracks in AI, biotechnology, computer graphics, computer science, nanotechnology and robotics. Students take college-level classes and labs in one track.

programs.title: Johns Hopkins Engineering Innovation
programs.org: Johns Hopkins University Whiting School of Engineering
programs.summary: Summer engineering courses on campus and online, in areas like mechanical and biomedical engineering, materials science and Python. Some courses give Johns Hopkins college credit.

programs.title: AI4ALL Ignite
programs.summary: A free, two-semester online program for US undergraduates in computing and technical majors. Students build an AI project with an industry mentor and get career preparation.
body: Who can apply: US undergraduates.

programs.title: Stanford AI4ALL
programs.summary: A summer program that introduces high school students to artificial intelligence through lectures, lab visits and small research projects with Stanford AI researchers. There is a residential session and an online session.

programs.title: Grainger Engineering Summer Camps (WYSE)
programs.org: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Worldwide Youth in Science and Engineering
programs.summary: About 20 one-week engineering camps at Illinois for middle and high school students, in areas like aerospace, computer science and chemical engineering. Students do projects and live on campus for some camps.

programs.title: Georgia Tech CEISMC Summer PEAKS
programs.org: Georgia Tech Center for Education Integrating Science, Mathematics and Computing
programs.summary: One- and two-week day programs at Georgia Tech for K-12 students. High school sessions cover engineering design, computing, robotics and makerspace tools.

programs.title: Michigan Math and Science Scholars (MMSS)
programs.summary: Two-week summer courses at the University of Michigan in math, physics, chemistry, biology and computing, taught by faculty. Students can attend one, two or three sessions.
body: Who can apply: Rising sophomores, juniors and seniors.

programs.title: Inspirit AI
programs.summary: Paid online AI courses for high school students, taught in small groups by university graduate students. Students learn Python and machine learning and build a project.

programs.title: Johns Hopkins Center for Talented Youth (CTY) Summer Programs
programs.org: Johns Hopkins University Center for Talented Youth
programs.summary: Three-week summer courses for advanced students in math, science, computer science, writing and humanities. There are day programs for grades 2 to 8, residential programs for grades 7 to 12, and online courses.
body: Who can apply: Qualifying test score or other evidence of advanced ability.

programs.title: Northwestern Center for Talent Development (CTD) Summer Programs
programs.org: Northwestern University Center for Talent Development
